records.title: Choosing, sharpening and cleaning pruning tools for a bush rose

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The thickness at which hand pruners give way to loppers differs between sources: three-quarters of an inch in two rose sources, half an inch in a general woody-plant text (C8). Sources name bypass pruners without giving a reason, and one recommends anvil pruners for dead wood (C9). Sources differ on what to disinfect with and how often, and none cites evidence of effectiveness (C10). No source compares sharp and blunt tools directly; the advice rests on practitioner agreement (AF-27).

items.text: Match the tool to the stem: bypass hand pruners for thin canes, loppers for thicker ones, and a pruning saw for the thickest or oldest canes.
Hand pruners are for stems up to about three-quarters of an inch (about 2 cm) thick. Use loppers or a saw above that.
Use bypass (scissor-action) pruners. Anvil pruners are fine for clearing dead wood only.
Keep your tools sharp and clean, so each cut is clean and doesn't crush the cane.
Wipe the blades with 70 percent alcohol between plants, and after cutting out diseased wood. A sensible precaution, not a strict rule.

records.title: Making a pruning cut on a bush rose: removing a whole stem, or shortening one back to a bud

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Distance above the bud (C2): most sources say about a quarter inch; a few say up to half an inch. Both are defensible answers to the same tradeoff (too close risks killing the bud; too far risks the stub dying back). All the quarter-inch sources are from the United States. Slant direction (C3): most sources say "away from the bud"; a few say "in the same direction as the bud", and it's unresolved whether that's the same technique. Whether angle and bud direction matter at all (C11): rose societies in South Australia and South Africa say they matter little, or recommend a straight cut; neither gives a reason. The approved default keeps the majority convention. Sealing (C4, AF-30, AF-35): most sources, including every UK and New Zealand source, don't mention it. Where rose sources recommend it, the reason is to keep cane-boring insects out of the soft pith, not to help the cut heal. General tree research finds that wound dressings don't help healing, which answers a different question. No trial of sealed against unsealed rose canes was found. Stubs (AF-29): five of the nine sources are about dead canes, so whether the rule applies equally to every kind of removal isn't directly addressed. Two kinds of cut (AF-31): only one of the three sources is rose-specific. Outward bud (AF-21): two sources allow an exception for a cane that already spreads sideways.

removeStem.text: Cut the stem off where it starts: at the base, at the bud union, or where it joins its parent stem. Don't leave a stub.

shorten.text: Cut just above a bud that faces outward, away from the centre of the bush.
Cut about a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) above the bud. Up to half an inch is also fine if you'd rather avoid the stub dying back.
Make the cut on a slant, at roughly 45 degrees, not flat.
Slant the cut away from the bud.

seal.text: On cuts roughly pencil-thick or larger, you can seal the end with wood glue, nail polish or pruning sealer, to keep cane-boring insects out. Thinner cuts don't need it.

records.title: Advisory: removing no more than about a third of a bush in one session (general pruning guidance, not rose-specific)

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: This is a general rule for shrubs and trees, not tested on roses. One rose-specific source recommends a hard, one-time renovation instead, which suggests the rule is a cautious default rather than a rose requirement (AF-40). The NC State wording is about a plant's crown in any one year, not about a single session (WEAKCONGESTED AF-18). No source links the choice between one hard cutback and a staged approach to a particular bush's condition (AF-40). A fifth source listed for AF-40 (Colorado State University, Adams County) couldn't be confirmed and isn't cited.

content.heading: How much to remove
content.label: General pruning guidance, not specific to roses

items.text: A general pruning rule for shrubs and trees is to remove no more than about a third of a plant's growth in one session. Removing more can stress the plant, drain its stored energy and cause a flush of uncontrolled regrowth.
One general source puts it as no more than a third of a plant's crown in any one year.
If an overgrown bush needs more than that, the same guidance spreads the work over two or three years, about a third at a time.
This rule hasn't been tested on roses, and at least one rose source recommends a single hard renovation instead. Treat it as a cautious guide, not a limit.

records.title: Growing-season care for a Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); general care outside pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Feeding and deadheading: when to stop depends on the region, and no single date is given (F4, F5). Mulch depth: sources give 2 to 4 inches (Source Register §3, matter 4). Watching for problems: this record doesn't diagnose anything (F6). The "notice first" framing rests on one source (F12). The claim that growing conditions cause most decline is also single-source (F13). Region: all sources are UK or US (ARC §5).

content.heading: Growing-season care

items.text: Water deeply and less often, rather than a little and often. In the growing season, aim for roughly 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) of water a week, counting rain, when it's dry.
Spread organic mulch about 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) deep around the base — bark, well-rotted manure, wood chips or pine needles — kept a few inches clear of the stems.
Start feeding in spring as new growth begins, feed again through summer, and stop by mid-to-late summer so new growth can toughen before winter. Stop earlier where winter comes earlier.
Remove faded flowers through the growing season to encourage more. Stop in early-to-mid autumn, so the rose can form hips and slow down for winter.
Watch for blackspot, powdery mildew, aphids and spider mites. Water at the base, or in the morning if you water from above, to keep the leaves drier.
Look over the leaves, buds and stems regularly for yellowing, spots, dropping leaves, stunted or twisted growth, or fewer flowers. Noticing early is the useful first step.
If your rose looks unwell, think about its growing conditions first: uneven watering, soggy soil or extreme weather. One extension service says these cause most decline.

content.disclosure: This care advice comes mainly from UK and US gardening services. Timings and amounts may differ where you live.

records.title: Caring for a recently planted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose that PKR-SGT-000002 has stopped (planted less than about three years ago, or establishment not shown)
common.preserved_uncertainty: F7 concerns roughly the first year. F2's closer watering covers roughly the first two years. The pruning wait (PKR-SGT-000002) is about three years or more. These are three different questions and are stated separately, not merged (ARC F2 limitations). The gate's own question is about three years, so item 1 is worded for the gardener to apply if the rose went in within about the past year.

content.heading: Caring for a recently planted rose

items.text: If your rose was planted within about the past year, leave as much of its leaves and stems as you can this first season. Only remove faded flowers, and don't cut stems for the vase. A new rose uses its leaves to make the energy it needs to grow roots.
Pay closer attention to watering for roughly the first two years after planting.
Full pruning usually waits until a rose has been in the ground about three years. I'll check this again next time.

records.title: Preparing a Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose for winter

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003), in an area with hard winter frosts
common.preserved_uncertainty: Winter mounding applies where winters bring hard frosts (F9). Mound heights vary between sources, from 8 to 18 inches, around the common 10–12 (Source Register §3, matter 4). Collars and wraps rest on two sources and are described particularly for climbing roses or exposed sites (F10). All sources are from the US (ARC §5).

content.heading: Preparing for winter
content.label: If your winters bring hard frosts…

items.text: Once the rose has had several hard frosts and gone dormant, mound soil, compost or mulch about 10–12 inches (25–30 cm) high around the base, covering the graft union. Remove the mound in spring once hard frosts have passed.
For colder or exposed spots, sources also describe a collar of tar paper or wire mesh filled with straw, pine bark or peat moss, or wrapping canes in burlap or evergreen boughs.
Water thoroughly after the first hard frost and before the ground freezes, and clear fallen leaves from around the plant before winter.

records.title: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The view that pruning does not kill a rose is expert opinion, not measured (AF-1). One commercial website disagrees, saying cutting back too far "could stress it out or even kill it" (AF-20, Very Low; C-1). Sources disagree on whether "weak" means the whole plant or a single shoot (C-2), and on renovating in one go or in stages (C-4). Newly planted roses are outside this record.

content.heading: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

items.text: Rose societies, rose growers and a botanic garden in New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US say pruning, even hard or badly done, doesn't kill an established rose.
Some of them add conditions: the rose is otherwise healthy, it isn't cut below the ground line, and its roots are intact.
The cut sources say can lose a rose is one made below the graft or below the ground line.
A weak or slow-growing rose is pruned less hard than a vigorous one. Within a bush, sources still cut single weak shoots back further or remove them.
Pruning before the frosts have passed risks frost damage to the new growth and dieback.
Sources describe any harm from pruning too hard as a short-term setback. One says the first year after a hard pruning is a recovery year.
An old or neglected rose can be brought back with hard pruning.
Pip's approach to a heavy renovation is to spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Some sources do it all in one go, and none gives a rule for choosing.
Sources give no signs or waiting time for judging recovery. If no new growth appears during the growing season, ask your local rose society.

records.title: Why isn't my rose flowering?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source gives a tested way to tell the causes apart, or says which is most common (R-1). Sources disagree on sun hours (C-1), on feeding (C-2), on where to cut a blind shoot (C-4), on first-season flowering (C-5), on how hard is too hard (C-6) and on chemical treatment of balling (C-7). Rose midge has no New Zealand or Australian source (R-3). Lower-confidence findings (potassium AF-7, heat AF-9, cold AF-10, hips AF-20, rootstock AF-32, pesticides AF-33) are not used in this answer.

items.text: Pip can't tell you which reason applies to your rose. Here are the reasons sources give, with what to look for and what they suggest.
Too little sun, or too much shade, means fewer flowers.
Sources give a minimum of four to eight hours of direct sun a day. Six is the most common figure.
Trees and shrubs nearby compete with a rose for light, water and food. Sources advise planting roses away from them.
Too much fertiliser, especially nitrogen, gives lots of leafy growth and few flowers.
Too little feeding is also given as a reason, and feeding as a remedy. Pip's care tips give the feeding pattern.
Too little water, or drought, reduces flowering. Sources describe pale, limp leaves, dropped leaves and small flowers.
Pruning too much, too little or at the wrong time is listed as a reason. No source says where too much begins.
Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers. Lighter pruning gives more, smaller ones.
Removing spent flowers from a repeat-flowering rose encourages more flowers.

If your rose flowered once in late spring or early summer and not again, it may be a once-flowering variety. Pip can't support those yet. A local rose society or garden centre can help, or you can check its type with Pip's rose-type questions.
Pruning a once-flowering rose before it flowers removes its flowers.
A blind shoot grows and leafs normally but has no flower bud at its tip.
The cause of blind shoots isn't known. Sources suggest weather, shade, over-feeding and big swings between day and night temperatures.
Sources cut a blind shoot back to get a new shoot that can flower. The RHS cuts it back by half to a strong bud. Others cut to the next leaf joint down, or to the next full five-leaflet leaf.
Buds that form but don't open after cool, wet weather may be "balled": the bud feels soft and its outer petals turn brown and papery.
Sources remove balled or rotting buds promptly, and suggest better air flow around the plant and watering at the base, not over the leaves.
Sources link spotted petals with grey fuzz to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.
Sources link brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, to thrips.
Sources link holes in buds, with caterpillars, to budworm.
Black spot (dark spots on the leaves, then yellowing and leaf drop) weakens a rose so it flowers less.
A photo alone can't show why a rose isn't flowering. Check these signs on the plant itself.

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning, or the removal-only session of PKR-SGT-000001 v1.1 §2.1

decision_notes.text: Remove it back into living tissue — white or pale-green pith and green bark — not just to the first sign of dead tissue.
If dieback carries on after repeated cuts, keep going toward the bud union, or remove the whole cane.

records.title: Crossing or rubbing stems — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Only 2 of about 16 sources give any rule for which of the two stems to remove (AF-7, Low). One source argues against deliberately opening the centre of the bush (C-1, unresolved; the majority view is recorded). Whether a gardener should wait when unsure which stem to remove was not addressed by any source (AF-8).

decision_notes.text: Remove the crossing or rubbing stem as ordinary dormant pruning.
Remove it completely, back to where it starts (the ground, the bud union, or the larger cane it grows from). Don't just shorten it.
If you need to choose which one, the few sources that give a rule say remove the weaker, thinner one and keep the stronger one.
Why: stems rubbing together damage each other's bark, which lets disease in.
Take care not to damage the stem you're keeping; cut a tangled stem out in sections rather than pulling it whole.

records.title: Damaged growth — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning, or the removal-only session of PKR-SGT-000001 v1.1 §2.1
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source defines "slight" versus "severe" precisely (AF-12). The answer is always to keep cutting down until healthy pith is found. The canker margin is worded "2–3 inches" or "well below" (AF-13). Disinfectant strength and how often to use it vary between sources (AF-15). Sources differ on how long to wait after frost damage (C-2).

decision_notes.text: Cut the damaged cane back until you reach healthy wood: white or pale-green pith. Brown, black or grey means keep cutting a little further down.
Slight damage: shorten just to healthy wood. Severe damage, or no living pith or buds below it: remove the whole cane at its base.
If it looks like canker or disease: cut well below the patch (commonly 2–3 inches, about 5–8 cm), clean your blades between cuts, and bin or burn the prunings.
If it looks like borer damage: cut below the damaged part until the pith is white or the hole is gone, then seal the fresh cut.

Frost or winter damage often doesn't show its full extent straight away. Sources advise waiting until live growth is emerging, so "Decide later" is the recommended choice for a frost-damaged cane. When you come back, I'll help you remove it even if the rose is growing.
Leave: sources advise cutting confirmed damage back to healthy wood.

records.title: Weak or congested growth — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The number of canes to keep varies by source and region, from 1–4 to 4–8 (C-2), so Pip gives a range. The sunscald caution comes from one source and applies to hot-summer climates (AF-18). The one-third caution comes from general (not rose-specific) advice about annual crown removal (AF-18). No source explains why weak canes should be removed before congestion is decided; the order follows how sources sequence the work (AF-14; U-6).

decision_notes.text: Weak cane: remove it completely, at its base or where it starts. Don't shorten it.
Crowded bush: remove whole canes, never part-shorten one. Keep the strongest, then aim for even spacing and an open, airy centre.
Keep roughly 3–7 strong canes, 4–6 typical, and fewer for a modest or young plant.
If the plant already looks weak or small, prune it lightly.
In hot-summer areas, leave some growth in the middle to shade the graft. Don't clear all the crowding at once.
Reaching inside the bush, wear eye protection and long-cuffed gloves.

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning

records.title: Rootstock sucker — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established grafted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or provisional Grandiflora rose
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on tearing versus cutting at the origin, and no trial compares them on roses (C-1; R-4). choices.label: Remove the sucker where it starts

decision_notes.text: Suckers draw strength from your rose and, left alone, can take it over.
Remove it early, while it's young — it's easier then.
Leave: sources advise removing confirmed suckers, because they weaken the rose.
If suckers keep coming back after removal, get experienced local help.

removal_method.text: Uncover the point where the sucker starts, clearing soil if needed, and remove it right there. Never cut it off at soil level — a sucker cut at the surface grows back.
Main method: with gloves on, grip the sucker as close to where it starts as you can and pull or tear it away. Tearing takes the hidden buds at its base with it, which makes regrowth less likely.
Alternative: some sources cut it cleanly, flush at the point where it starts. Sources disagree on which works better; both agree it must go at the origin.
Support the stem with one hand; afterwards refill the soil and firm it gently around the base.
Take care around the base when weeding or digging — root damage is linked with suckering.

records.title: Dead vs. living wood

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: No Comparison Image PKR exists yet (documented gap, Founder decision 24 August 2026). Pith colour needs a cut and flexibility needs a bend, so neither can be judged from a photo.

content.look_for: Let's look for dead wood. Dead canes are usually brown, grey, black or shrivelled rather than green, and have no plump buds anywhere along them.

criteria.text: Bark colour: green suggests living; brown, grey, black or shrivelled suggests dead. Older or bronze canes can mislead.
Buds: plump visible buds suggest living; none anywhere suggests dead.
Sunken patches or lesions may be canker, not routine dead wood.
The surest check is the pith once cut: white or pale green is living; brown, grey or black is dead.
A living cane bends; a dead one is brittle and snaps.

content.photo_limit: A photo can't show the pith inside the cane or how it bends — check those on the plant.
content.confirm_question: Find that cane on your rose and look at it closely. Is it dead?
content.not_sure_guidance: Look again at the cane on the plant itself — its buds and its bark colour, right down low.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more dead canes?

criteria.text: A stem crossing another is a candidate. Crossing and rubbing are looked for together.
Bark damage, wear or a flattened face where two stems touch: treat as rubbing.
Stems close together with no contact or wear: treat as crossing, not rubbing.

records.title: Damaged growth

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Causes aren't equally evidenced: sunscald rests on one source, and rodent and snow damage on one each (AF-2). No test exists for a split that isn't visible from outside (AF-6). Experts themselves disagree on whether canker can be diagnosed from a photo (C-3), so Pip always states its confidence. Sources are UK, US and Australian.

content.look_for: Now let's look for damaged growth — canes that are injured or diseased but not simply dead.

criteria.text: Canker: tan to purplish-brown sunken patches with cracking edges, tiny black dots, or dieback above a patch that rings the cane.
Frost or winter injury: browned or blackened tips and discoloured canes. Confirming it needs a cut into the pith.
Physical damage: a visibly broken cane, or worn, rubbed bark where canes touch.
Borer: a new tip that suddenly wilts, an entry hole, or slight swelling. A hole in the end of an old pruning cut is often a harmless wasp nest.
Not damage: mossy or spiny insect galls are generally harmless, and red, purple or yellow spots on young canes can be their normal colour.

content.photo_limit: A photo can show outside signs, but not what's happening inside the cane. If it's unclear, look closely at the plant rather than taking another photo.
content.confirm_question: Find that cane on your rose. Can you see damage like this?
content.not_sure_guidance: Look closely at that spot on the plant itself, not at a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more damaged stems?

records.title: Weak or congested growth

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The two sources that put a number on "pencil thickness" disagree (about 6 mm versus 10 mm, C-1), so Pip uses no number. Why canes become weak is thinly evidenced; one source links congestion to weak growth, and one links old age to it (AF-2, Low). No source describes weak canes as arching or flopping, so that isn't used as a sign (U-2).

content.look_for: Let's look for weak canes — thinner than a pencil, twiggy or unproductive — and at whether the middle of the bush is crowded.

criteria.text: A cane thinner than about a pencil is a candidate weak cane. No number is used.
Twiggy or unproductive growth, with thin tips rather than full, lush canes.
Crowded: the bush is densely packed, especially at ground level, rather than open in the middle.
A thin cane with brown or reddish thorns may be this season's new growth rather than a weak cane.

content.photo_limit: Without a size reference, thickness can't be judged from a photo — hold a coin or pencil beside the cane. No photo can rule out crowding at the back of the bush.
content.confirm_question: Check the cane against a pencil, and look at the middle of the bush from more than one side. Is it weak, or is the bush crowded?
content.not_sure_guidance: Take a photo with a coin or pencil beside the cane, or look at the middle from another side, then check again.

records.title: The main framework to retain

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning

content.look_for: Finally, let's choose the framework to keep: the strong canes spread around the base that will form the shape of your rose.

criteria.text: Keeper canes: strong, healthy, vigorous canes, generally the younger ones.
Target shape: an open centre, with kept canes spread evenly around the base, like a vase or the spokes of a wheel.
Old wood: grey, rough, scaly or crusty bark, sometimes with worn prickles.
New shoots from the base are a sign of good health and a way to renew the framework.
Keep your rose's own new canes from the base. First check where each starts: a shoot from below the bud union is a sucker.

records.title: Rootstock suckers — shoots from below the bud union

common.applies_to: Established grafted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or provisional Grandiflora rose (passed PKR-SGT-000003). Any season (Founder decision D1(b)); PKR-SGT-000002 applies. Dormant session: point of origin only. Growing season: supporting signs may be added.
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source describes recognising a sucker on a dormant, leafless rose other than by where it starts (AF-10, Low). Sources disagree on how dependable leaf clues are (C-2), and rootstocks differ by country (AF-9; New Zealand mainly uses *Rosa multiflora* or strains of it), so Pip gives no rootstock-specific cues (R-3 default). One source says a rootstock stub left above the union can also sucker (AF-14, Low; C-6); this isn't used to classify shoots. No source gives a prickle or cane rule (AF-8). No source says what a photo can establish (R-2). Sources are UK, US, Australian and New Zealand.

content.look_for: Let's check for suckers. A sucker is a shoot from the rootstock your rose was grafted onto, below the bud union — the knobbly join near the base. It isn't your rose's own new cane.

criteria.text: Where the shoot starts is the deciding check: below the bud union is a sucker; at the union or just above it is your rose's own new cane, which you keep.
A sucker can start below the soil, sometimes a little away from the plant.
Planting depth varies, so the bud union may be above, at or below the soil.

content.photo_limit: A photo can't show where a shoot starts, especially under the soil. I never decide a shoot is a sucker from a photo.
content.confirm_question: Follow the shoot down with your fingers. Does it start below the bud union, or at or above it?
content.doesnt_match_label: At or above the bud union
content.doesnt_match_note: That's your rose's own new cane. Keep it — the rose's own basal canes are valuable. It's considered in the framework step.
content.not_sure_guidance: That's alright. It's easy to confuse these, even for experienced gardeners. Look again at where the shoot starts, on the plant, not in a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more shoots like this coming from the base?

sucker_steps.hasShoot: Is there a shoot coming from the base of your rose, or from the ground near it?
sucker_steps.unionVisible: Can you see the bud union — the knobbly join near the base where your rose was grafted?
sucker_steps.noUnion: Then I won't call it a sucker. The union may just be buried. If you like, gently clear a little soil and look again — otherwise leave the shoot, and ask experienced local help if you're concerned.
sucker_steps.ownRoot: If you know your rose grows on its own roots (it wasn't grafted), shoots from the base are the same rose, so none is a sucker — keep them.
sucker_steps.supporting: In the growing season only, these can help you look, but never decide on their own: sucker leaves are often paler or smaller or have a different number of leaflets (though the "seven leaflets" rule isn't reliable); sucker flowers differ from your rose's; suckers are often unusually vigorous, straight and tall.

records.title: Blind shoots — healthy shoots with no flower bud at the tip

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (passed PKR-SGT-000003), in the growing season

content.look_for: Let's check for blind shoots. A blind shoot grows and leafs normally, but has no flower bud at its tip.

criteria.text: The shoot and its leaves can look perfectly healthy; what's missing is a flower bud at the tip.
The tip may look empty, or dried up.
Nobody knows for certain what causes blind shoots.

content.photo_limit: I can't confirm a blind shoot from a photo. Look at the tip of the shoot itself.
content.confirm_question: Look closely at the very tip of the shoot. Is there a flower bud there?

content.not_sure_guidance: That's alright. Look again at the tip on the plant, not in a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more shoots like this, with leaves but no bud at the tip?

records.title: Dormancy gate — is the rose in the window for structural pruning?

common.applies_to: Established bush rose. Prerequisite for structural and whole-bush pruning (PKR-OBS/DEC-000002, 000003, 000005, 000006, and any shortening or shaping of healthy canes). Does not govern removal of wood confirmed dead, damaged or diseased (PKR-DEC-000001, PKR-DEC-000004), which follows the removal-only session.
common.preserved_uncertainty: AF-3 (Moderate): in mild or warm-winter climates, full leaf loss may not occur and premature bud break is a documented risk — the gardener should judge dormancy by bud state specifically, not by whether leaves are present. A follow-up commission (FRD-BUSHROSE-DORMANCY-02, submitted alongside this package) is testing whether the bud-swell signal itself needs a stated mild-climate exception; this gate's wording will be revised if that research changes the picture.

content.question: Look closely at the dormant buds along your rose's canes. Has active new growth already begun — buds swelling, breaking open, or new leaves emerging anywhere on the plant — or does the plant still appear dormant?
content.caveat: If your climate is mild or unusually warm, judge this by bud state specifically — not by whether the leaves have dropped. In milder climates a rose doesn't always lose all its leaves, and buds can sometimes break earlier than expected.

answers.dormant: Still dormant — buds are tight and closed, or just beginning to swell; no new leaves have opened anywhere
answers.growing: Active new growth is already well underway — leaves have opened and new shoots are clearly growing

content.notSureFallback: That's alright — have another look at the buds specifically, not the leaves: are they still tight and closed, or have any started to swell or open? If you're still not certain after a closer look, the safest choice is to treat the rose as not quite ready yet, and check back in a week or two.

intro.text: Your rose is already growing, so this is not the time for full pruning. Pruning hard now can cost you flowers. But you can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased.

removalOnly.notSureIntro: Since we can't be sure your rose is still dormant, we'll leave full pruning for now — check back in a week or two. You can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased today.

conditions.text: Remove only the wood you've confirmed. Don't shorten or shape healthy canes today.
Go gently and avoid damaging the new leaves and shoots.
Cut back until the pith is white or pale green, exactly as at any other time.
For anything that looks like canker or disease, the usual care applies: cut well below the affected part, clean your blades, and bin the prunings.

lateSeason.text: Late in the season (advice only): sources advise against pruning late in the growing season, because it can encourage new growth that winter cold may damage. Diseased wood is the exception — remove it whenever you find it. Sources don't say whether dead (as distinct from diseased) wood is exempt.
